To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ability of vascular endothelial cell (EC) sprouts to orient to vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF) is dependent on the surrounding biomaterial matrix, and that less dense matrices promote VEGF-mediated sprout alignment and navigation.
the ability of stable VEGF gradients to regulate endothelial cell sprout orientation during angiogenesis is biomaterial dependent.

the ability of vascular endothelial cells to respond to vascular endothelial growth factors depends on the density of collagen and fibronectin in the surrounding matrix, and that these matrix effects can be probed using microfluidic platforms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how cells respond to the physical and chemical properties of their surroundings and how these interactions influence the formation and maintenance of tissues.
how biomaterials regulate the pathfinding behavior of endothelial sprouts.
the development of new biomaterials that can be used for the regeneration of tissues.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
VEGF gradients are a necessary but not sufficient condition for endothelial sprouting.
VEGF gradients can induce pathfinding behaviors in endothelial cells, which are dependent on the density of biomaterials.

VEGF gradients can be used to direct the orientation of endothelial sprouts, but that the ability of these gradients to do so is dependent upon the mechanical properties of the biomaterials within which sprouting is occurring.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ability of biomaterials to promote angiogenesis depends on their ability to regulate the biomechanical and molecular signaling pathways that control the pathfinding of endothelial sprouts during angiogenesis.
the ability of a VEGF gradient to regulate sprout pathfinding is biomaterial dependent, and that this ability is related to the ability of the biomaterial to support endothelial cell migration.

VEGF gradients induce different types of coordinated cellular movements in different types of matrices and that this can have significant consequences on the ability of endothelial cells to properly navigate towards a VEGF source.
The main takeaway from our work is that

biomaterials that are used to promote angiogenesis must be able to support VEGF-induced endothelial sprout alignment and navigation to ensure that the newly formed vascular networks are properly oriented to support tissue regeneration.
the matrix microenvironment can regulate how cells respond to VEGF gradients.
VEGF gradients can induce different types of coordinated endothelial cell movements depending on matrix density.
